text: Everything this course has governed so far — catalogs, schemas, tables — lives under one namespace. Registered ML models get exactly the same treatment, not a separate, ungoverned registry off to the side.

A registered model's name is catalog-dot-schema-dot-model — the same three-level namespace a table uses. Point MLflow at Unity Catalog with set_registry_uri "databricks-uc", and a model inherits the same owners, the same USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA requirements, the same audit trail as everything else in that schema.

Registering is a dialog choice: Unity Catalog, not the legacy Workspace Model Registry. The destination is a three-level name, exactly like creating a table — here, searching for "iris model" resolves to prod-dot-ml underscore team-dot-iris underscore model.
Once registered, the model gets its own Catalog Explorer page — version history, owner, a Permissions tab. Same page shape as a table in the same schema, not a different tool to learn.

The legacy registry used fixed stages — Staging, Production, Archived. Unity Catalog replaces that with aliases: a mutable pointer you name yourself, like Champion for the current production version. Promoting a new version is one call that moves the alias — serving code always asks for at-Champion, nothing else changes.

And because training code can log its input dataset, Unity Catalog draws a real lineage line from a model version back to the table it was trained on — the same lineage mechanism Chapter 4 covered for tables, now showing up on the model's own Lineage tab.

A model is governed like a table because, inside Unity Catalog, it basically is one: same namespace, same grants, same lineage. Next lesson: migrating existing Hive metastore tables — and these same models — into Unity Catalog in the first place.
